title: Turibius of Mongrovejo (23 March)
hookLine: a lawyer made archbishop of Lima who walked his diocese and stood up for the Indigenous people in it

cards: A lawyer is sitting at his desk in Spain, a layman, a judge in a church court, when a letter arrives from the king. The archbishop's chair in Lima, across the ocean in Peru, is empty, and they want him in it.
He isn't a priest. He writes back with reasons he's the wrong man. The reasons are not accepted.
So he is ordained, made a bishop, and sent across the sea to a diocese of mountains, deserts and coast, full of people whose languages he doesn't speak. He could have run it from a desk.
His desk is about to become a mule.

teach.h: AN ARCHBISHOP ON FOOT AND BY MULE.
teach.b: Turibius took the job, and then he took to the road.

Tradition says he spent years of his time as archbishop away from Lima, on foot and by mule, up into the Andes and down into the valleys, to villages far from any cathedral. He slept where he could and ate what was there.
And he learned. He studied Quechua, a language spoken by people he served, so he could talk with them himself, not only through an interpreter.
Under his leadership the church in Lima prepared a catechism in Indigenous languages, so the faith could be taught in the people's own words. What he found on the road was hard to look at.
Spanish officials and landholders were abusing the Indigenous people, taking their labor and their land, and some clergy looked away.

teach.h: HE NAMED THE ABUSE HE SAW.
teach.b: Turibius named it. He held church councils that set rules for the clergy and pressed for justice, and he clashed with powerful men who preferred him in the capital.
In the Gospel of John, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "I am the good shepherd; and I know mine, and mine know me." You can't know a flock you've never met. That was his whole method.
Tradition says he died on the road, on one more visit, far from his cathedral.

teach.h: I KNOW MINE, AND MINE KNOW ME.
teach.b: The Church honors him as a patron of the bishops of Latin America. His title says archbishop. His feet say pastor.

how: Catholics keep Turibius's optional memorial in March, and in Peru and across Latin America he is honored as a model of a bishop who went out to his people.

games.q: you're Turibius, the new archbishop. your diocese runs from the coast up into the Andes, and the roads are brutal. what do you do?

games.why: he went himself, again and again, and tradition says he died on the road, far from his cathedral.

practice: Bring to mind someone you mostly reach through a screen: a grandparent, a neighbor, a friend across town, someone who's been unwell. Picture the actual visit, the door you'd knock on, what you'd bring, and how you'd simply listen.
If you pray, hold that person before God; if you don't, just keep their face in mind.

wordCard.voice: Quechua, the language Turibius of Mongrovejo learned to speak with his people. A lawyer made archbishop of Lima, he crossed his diocese to meet them, and stood up for them.

carryVoice: Your line: he walked it all. A shepherd gets to know the flock by going to meet it. Day nine hundred seventy-seven, done.
